knowledge_point.title: Determining Whether a Vector Lies on a Plane

question.:question/problem:
Determine whether $\mathbf{u}$ lies on the plane $\Pi:\mathbf{r}=s\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{c}$, where $s,t\in\mathbb{R}$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{b}&=\langle 0, 1, 3\rangle \\ \mathbf{c}&=\langle 1, 0, 1\rangle \\ \mathbf{u}&=\langle 2, 1, 5\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

If it does, select the value of $s\cdot t$ in $\mathbf{u}=s\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{c}$. Otherwise, select the statement that $\mathbf{u}$ does not lie on $\Pi$.

Use the component equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}t &=2 \\ s &=1 \\ 3s+t &=5\end{aligned}\right.
$$

**Check all three coordinates.** Use the equations that isolate the coefficients, then verify the remaining equation.
question.:question/worked-solution:
By definition, $\mathbf{u}\in\Pi$ exactly when the same values of $s$ and $t$ satisfy all three coordinate equations. Expanding the vector equation gives

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}t &=2 \\ s &=1 \\ 3s+t &=5\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Set up the augmented matrix:

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 & 5\end{array}\right]
$$

Apply $R_1 \leftrightarrow R_2$, then $R_3 \leftarrow R_3-(3)R_1$, then $R_3 \leftarrow R_3-(1)R_2$:

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]
$$

The last row is $0=0$, so it adds no restriction. Back substitute in the two nonzero rows:

$$
\begin{aligned}t&=\frac{2}{1}=2 \\ s&=\frac{1-(0)(2)}{1}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Verify every coordinate:

$$
\begin{aligned}(1)(0)+(2)(1)&=2=2 \\ (1)(1)+(2)(0)&=1=1 \\ (1)(3)+(2)(1)&=5=5\end{aligned}
$$

All three coordinates agree, so the vector lies on the plane. Therefore,

$$
s\cdot t=(1)\cdot(2)=2.
$$

:answer-field/choices.:answer/feedback: The pair $s=1,t=2$ satisfies all three coordinates; the vector lies on the plane.
Correct. The common pair satisfies all three equations and gives $s\cdot t=2$.

knowledge_point.title: Determining Whether a Vector Lies on a Plane

question.:question/problem:
Determine whether $\mathbf{u}$ lies on the plane $\Pi:\mathbf{r}=s\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{c}$, where $s,t\in\mathbb{R}$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{b}&=\langle -3, 1, 0\rangle \\ \mathbf{c}&=\langle -2, 0, 1\rangle \\ \mathbf{u}&=\langle 11, -3, -1\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

If it does, select the value of $s\cdot t$ in $\mathbf{u}=s\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{c}$. Otherwise, select the statement that $\mathbf{u}$ does not lie on $\Pi$.

Use the component equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-3s-2t &=11 \\ s &=-3 \\ t &=-1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

**Check all three coordinates.** Use the equations that isolate the coefficients, then verify the remaining equation.
question.:question/worked-solution:
By definition, $\mathbf{u}\in\Pi$ exactly when the same values of $s$ and $t$ satisfy all three coordinate equations. Expanding the vector equation gives

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-3s-2t &=11 \\ s &=-3 \\ t &=-1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Set up the augmented matrix:

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-3 & -2 & 11 \\ 1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{array}\right]
$$

Apply $R_2 \leftarrow R_2-\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)R_1$, then $R_3 \leftarrow R_3-\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right)R_2$:

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-3 & -2 & 11 \\ 0 & -\frac{2}{3} & \frac{2}{3} \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]
$$

The last row is $0=0$, so it adds no restriction. Back substitute in the two nonzero rows:

$$
\begin{aligned}t&=\frac{\frac{2}{3}}{-\frac{2}{3}}=-1 \\ s&=\frac{11-(-2)(-1)}{-3}=-3\end{aligned}
$$

Verify every coordinate:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-3)(-3)+(-1)(-2)&=11=11 \\ (-3)(1)+(-1)(0)&=-3=-3 \\ (-3)(0)+(-1)(1)&=-1=-1\end{aligned}
$$

All three coordinates agree, so the vector lies on the plane. Therefore,

$$
s\cdot t=(-3)\cdot(-1)=3.
$$

:answer-field/choices.:answer/feedback: This is $t$ alone; the question asks for $s\cdot t$.
The pair $s=-3,t=-1$ satisfies all three coordinates; the vector lies on the plane.
This is $s$ alone; the question asks for $s\cdot t$.
Correct. The common pair satisfies all three equations and gives $s\cdot t=3$.

knowledge_point.title: Determining Whether a Vector Lies on a Plane

question.:question/problem:
Determine whether $\mathbf{u}$ lies on the plane $\Pi:\mathbf{r}=s\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{c}$, where $s,t\in\mathbb{R}$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{b}&=\langle -2, 0, 1\rangle \\ \mathbf{c}&=\langle -3, 1, 0\rangle \\ \mathbf{u}&=\langle 3, -2, 2\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

If it does, select the value of $s\cdot t$ in $\mathbf{u}=s\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{c}$. Otherwise, select the statement that $\mathbf{u}$ does not lie on $\Pi$.

Use the component equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-2s-3t &=3 \\ t &=-2 \\ s &=2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

**Check all three coordinates.** Use the equations that isolate the coefficients, then verify the remaining equation.
question.:question/worked-solution:
By definition, $\mathbf{u}\in\Pi$ exactly when the same values of $s$ and $t$ satisfy all three coordinate equations. Expanding the vector equation gives

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-2s-3t &=3 \\ t &=-2 \\ s &=2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Set up the augmented matrix:

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-2 & -3 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & 0 & 2\end{array}\right]
$$

Apply $R_3 \leftarrow R_3-\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)R_1$, then $R_3 \leftarrow R_3-\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right)R_2$:

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-2 & -3 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{2}\end{array}\right]
$$

The last row gives $0=\frac{1}{2}$, a contradiction. No pair satisfies all three equations. Thus $\mathbf{u}$ does not lie on $\Pi$. A product obtained from only two coordinates is not a valid answer.

:answer-field/choices.:answer/feedback: Check all three coordinates before giving a product; the system has no common solution.

Correct. The coordinate system is inconsistent.
